introduction: Timon makes generosity the centre of his life in Athens, paying debts, supporting marriages and entertaining a circle that praises his boundless friendship. His steward and the abrasive Apemantus see dangers that his gratitude to his friends keeps him from admitting. When his resources fail, the meaning of those relationships comes under pressure. Alongside his private financial crisis, Alcibiades confronts the city's rulers over mercy and justice, linking questions of personal obligation to the use and abuse of public power.

fullSynopsis.text: Timon's house in Athens attracts artists, merchants, lords and senators who profit from his generosity. He pays the imprisoned Ventidius's debt and supplies his servant Lucilius with enough wealth to secure a marriage. At a lavish banquet he refuses Ventidius's offered repayment, welcomes entertainment and distributes further gifts. The cynical Apemantus warns that the guests consume their host's fortune and will abandon him when it fails. Timon instead celebrates friendship as a shared store of affection and resources. His steward Flavius sees that gifts are being made from empty coffers, but Timon postpones hearing him.

Creditors demand payment, and Flavius finally makes Timon confront his debts. His lands are already pledged or lost, and what remains cannot meet his obligations. Timon insists that he has given unwisely rather than dishonourably and believes his friends will now demonstrate their love. He sends servants to Lucullus, Lucius and Sempronius and seeks repayment from Ventidius. The senators have already refused assistance. Lucullus tries to bribe the messenger into pretending they never met; Lucius invents a financial excuse; Sempronius claims insult at being approached after others. The servant reports that Ventidius, too, has refused.

As the creditors' servants beset his house, Timon's confidence turns to rage. He invites his former guests to one final feast, serves covered dishes of lukewarm water, denounces their friendship and throws the water in their faces before driving them out. Meanwhile Alcibiades petitions the senate for mercy towards a soldier condemned for killing a man. The senators reject his arguments and banish Alcibiades himself when he persists. He resolves to raise his discontented troops against Athens. Timon also leaves the city, stripping off its claims upon him and calling for the destruction of its institutions and people.

Flavius shares his remaining money among the dismissed servants and seeks Timon in the wilderness. Digging for roots near the sea, Timon unexpectedly uncovers gold. He sees in it the power to reverse moral and social distinctions and decides to turn it against mankind. When Alcibiades passes with Phrynia and Timandra, Timon finances his army and urges indiscriminate slaughter in Athens. Alcibiades accepts the money but rejects that counsel. Timon gives the women gold while urging them to spread disease. Apemantus visits and challenges the authenticity of Timon's new misanthropy; their dispute ends in insults and a thrown stone.

Timon gives money to bandits while declaring that theft pervades nature, professions and law. His encouragement unsettles them, and some speak of abandoning robbery. Flavius offers his wealth and continuing service, forcing Timon to acknowledge one honest man as an exception to his hatred. Yet he dismisses the steward with gold and commands to avoid humanity. Hearing of his treasure, the Poet and Painter come promising renewed service; Timon exposes their self-interest and drives them off. Athens, threatened by Alcibiades, offers Timon honours, wealth and military command. He rejects the appeal, recommending that his countrymen hang themselves from his tree instead.

Timon withdraws to prepare his grave by the sea. A soldier seeking him finds that he is dead and takes an impression of his epitaph, without the play showing how he died. At Athens's walls, the senators plead that the whole city should not suffer for particular wrongdoers. Alcibiades agrees to limit punishment to his and Timon's designated enemies and to subject his troops to public law. The soldier brings the news of Timon's death, and Alcibiades reads the bitter inscription. He mourns the noble man behind its hatred, then enters Athens promising to join military strength with peace. Timon's personal refusal of reconciliation ends beside the city's negotiated survival.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Poet, Painter, Jeweller and Merchant discuss the wealthy Timon and the rewards his patronage offers. Timon pays Ventidius's prison debt and provides Lucilius with the means to marry an old Athenian's daughter. Apemantus interrupts the exchanges with insults and warnings about flattery. At the feast, Timon refuses repayment from the newly wealthy Ventidius and speaks emotionally of the support his friends would provide in need. A masque and dancing accompany the lavish hospitality, and more presents provoke further gifts in return. Flavius privately laments the empty treasury and mounting debts. Timon postpones hearing his concerns and refuses to listen when Apemantus condemns the display.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: A senator calculates Timon's debts and sends Caphis to demand repayment without accepting delay or courteous evasion. Other creditors' servants gather at Timon's house and confront him as he returns from hunting. While Apemantus and a Fool mock their trade, Flavius prepares to tell his master the truth. He explains that Timon has repeatedly refused accounts, that his property is heavily committed and that his remaining means cannot satisfy his debts. Timon acknowledges imprudence but trusts in friendship. He sends servants to request loans from several beneficiaries and orders an approach to Ventidius for the original five talents. Flavius reports that the senators have already declined to help.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Lucullus, Lucius and Sempronius refuse Timon's requests, each disguising ingratitude with a different excuse; Ventidius's refusal is also reported. Their conduct provokes bitter responses from servants and observers. Creditors' men press for payment until Timon bursts out in rage, then orders another feast despite Flavius's warnings. In the senate, Alcibiades seeks mercy for a condemned soldier, but his insistence earns him banishment and prompts plans of armed revenge. Timon's former friends accept his renewed invitation, hoping his apparent need was merely a test. Instead he serves lukewarm water, attacks their false professions, splashes them and drives them out. He renounces Athens and all humanity.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Timon curses Athens and leaves for the woods. His servants grieve, and Flavius distributes his remaining wealth before following his master. Timon digs for roots and discovers gold, whose corrupting power he denounces. He gives Alcibiades money to wage war on Athens and demands universal slaughter, which the captain refuses to promise. Phrynia and Timandra receive gold with exhortations to spread disease. Apemantus accuses Timon of adopting misanthropy only because fortune has changed; their quarrel ends violently. Timon also funds bandits, but his picture of universal theft makes some reconsider their trade. Flavius's faithful grief moves Timon to recognize his honesty, though he still sends him away.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: The Poet and Painter return after hearing that Timon has gold, offering promises of work and loyalty. He detects their interest in profit and drives them away. Senators then offer restoration, honours and command if he will defend Athens from Alcibiades. Timon rejects them and offers his tree for the citizens to hang themselves. He describes his intended seaside grave and withdraws. A soldier subsequently finds him dead and copies the inscription. Facing the army, the senators seek limited punishment rather than general destruction. Alcibiades accepts that distinction and guarantees lawful conduct by his men. He hears of Timon's death, reads the epitaph and enters Athens promising to temper war with peace.
